data.name: Martial Arts Brutality
data.detailed_description:
Enter the savage world of Martial Arts Brutality.

In this F2P turn based tactical card fighter, you will learn the secrets of Kung Fu, master control of your formidable Chi Energy and perfect the legendary Dim Mak death touch.

Discover and collect technique cards, upgrade their awesome powers, and build ultimate fighting decks.
Fight online with or against friends, mock and insult them using the unique taunt system.
Inflict horrific injuries on you opponents and execute many different KO types as you battle your way to becoming a Dragon Grand Master.
Is your inner warrior ready to meet the challenge? The brutal world of the Martial Arts awaits...

Features
  • A unique blend of tactical card play and real time attacking and defensive mechanics
  • Detailed human body model allows for horrific injuries and numerous brutal KO types.
  • Watch the vicious action unfold with a full fight replay system
  • Discover and collect martial arts cards, including Chi strikes and forbidden Dim Mak techniques.
  • Master a number of styles, including Shaolin Kung Fu, Wing Chun, Shotokan Karate and Taekwondo
  • Insane 8 player brawls. ‘Every man for himself’ and team fights.
  • Battle against friends and taunt them along the way!

reviews.review:
[i][b]Disclosure:[/b] I have completed this game once before on the Android.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] A fun card battler/QTE swiping hybrid. Ultimately made for touchscreen devices so using the mouse can be not as smooth. Mostly bug free and the barebones story isn't much to look at. Has lots of microtransactions, but for a free game, especially one without ads, it is quite fun to play, especially, the four quests involving the main campaign, and even the multiplayer modes. Pretty fun as a way to pass the time.[/i]

[hr][/hr]

Martial Arts Brutality is a pretty fun card battler/ QTE swiping hybrid. It was originally designed for touchscreen devices, but it works well enough with the mouse. The difficulty curve might be just a bit higher is all. There isn't a lot to this game apart from the gameplay itself and the way it showcases the brutality of martial arts in an apt representation of the title. There is a strategic edge to it in addition to the swiping action as well as a focus on building a reliable deck to achieve your intended means. All in all, it's a pretty fun title for a free game with microtransactions.

The game doesn't really have much in the way of a storyline. There are four quests as far as the campaign is concerned wherein the first one partially encompasses the tutorial and gently eases the players into the mechanics of the game. The rest of three quests are different, disjoint scenarios. Apart from a barebones plotline, though, there is little to no narration to the events within the game. It is, by all means, meant to be enjoyed for the gameplay itself.

The gameplay is a hybrid between a deck-builder and a QTE swiper. Being a deck-builder combined with the fact that the levels have certain challenges to complete lends the game an edge of strategy as well wherein you must not only obtain the right cards, but also play them well from a thought out deck that is not going to leave you defenseless or cripple your offensive while you try to juggle the objectives that you must complete. There are two phases to every fight: attacking and defending, which takes place in turns. When you're attacking, you have a selection of cards to choose from and you must strategise their use in order to meet the goal that you're trying to achieve within the limited time alloted to you during your turn. Success or failiure depends upon how well you can swipe out the pattern indicated on screen while activating a card. The strategic aspect to attacking comes from using cards that target the same body system for success. There are various ways to defeat opponents, ranging from the simple KO using multiple attacks to the head, the humble Cardiac Arrest via multiple attacks to the heart, or putting them in a simple Coma by attacking the brain. But you can get even more creative with your attacks and suffocate them or paralyse them by attacks to the lungs or the spine. You can also take the further complex route of crippling them using attacks to the arms or legs, or even go for multiple joints. Or you can simply sit back and blind them with attacks to the eyes. But for all intents and purposes, the goal of success through attacks in this game is to target various body systems to incapacitate your enemies and therein lies not only the brutality of the game, but also its depth. There are also buffs and debuffs for you to use in between all of these. Defence, on the other hand, is left entirely up to your reaction time. You need to swipe against incoming attacks to nullify them, and you can even counter said attacks. Attacks to limbs have their definitely advantage in nullifying cards that require the use of said limbs and otherwise slowing said attacks. There is also an RPG system where you can purchase upgrades for your character in exchange for points obtained through the completion of challenges.

The levels start out pretty easy, but get more and more difficult with time, as is to be expected. The enemy attacks get faster and they get tankier. Not only that, but even the challenges get more specific with time, leaving you to create multiple decks just to achieve the objectives of the levels. But there really isn't much progression in the game apart from that, and the levels in the quests are more or less relevant to the story which doesn't seem to have much direction to it. Sometimes, you might be fighting one foe. At others, you might be fighting three. At some points, you could teaming up with three other folks to take down one enemy, and at times, you could be interfering in a battle between two teams of four where everyone is your enemy for no good reason.

Despite there being little progression to the structure of challenges, the game does reward you quite generously and quite often, especially for a free title. It has loads and loads of microtransactions, but even getting the free rewards isn't particularly grindy. That being said, completing some of the challenges might require you to get greater amounts of cards that target certain body systems and obtaining them can be a bit difficult with just the free tier rewards. Not only that, but some of these other challenges actually require you to pay to complete them by requiring you to adopt a certain fighting style during the battle wherein each style has its own benefits and drawbacks. The game isn't particularly grindy at all to enjoy, but it is going to be really grindy if you're looking at 100% completion.

The graphics in the game are pretty simple. They're effectively 2D sprites with minimal, blurry animation, and it honestly works out well given the theme. It mostly relies on the the text desciprtions of escalating amounts of damage to get the point across. Sometimes, you might see bones sticking out of the other guy when they're damaged enough. The art style isn't particularly impressive, but if it was, this game might not have become a mobile game in the first place. The soundtracks sound pretty amazing, but the ending credits don't really mention them, pointing to the fact that they might be using unlicensed ripoffs of sountracks from SoundCloud or something.

As far as bugs are concerned, there are almost none, expect for the occasional lack of swipes and "taps" not being detected, which is honestly a problem I'm only facing in this port and have never encountered while playing it on the Android. Apart from that, some of the foreground elements might cover the action in certain stages like the Forest and might even draw themselves over the characters' faces during dialogue.

All in all, Martial Arts Brutality is a pretty fun game to play. It is an ideal way to pass the time, and given the hybrid deck-building and arcade QTE swiping mechanics, I can see myself returning to it from time to time. It isn't particularly grindy and pretty rewarding for a game with microtransactions, but it will cost you money for 100% completion if you're chasing any such thing. For all the the gameplay is worth, it is a pretty fun title, all things considered.
